incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
A South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience has become a victim of artificial intelligence fraud targeting vulnerable immigrants. Angel Leal discovered that scammers created hundreds of fake social media profiles and AI-generated videos using his likeness to promote fraudulent immigration services. The videos falsely advertise services such as US residency assistance for undocumented immigrants in exchange for cash payments of around $2,200. Leal first learned of the scheme when potential clients began calling his office, and the situation has escalated significantly over the past three months.

To combat the fraud, Leal's office hired an anti-piracy company that successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles across social media platforms, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. The scams typically direct victims through social media videos to WhatsApp numbers, where fraudsters exchange fake contracts and request payments via Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App. Leal warns immigrants to verify identities before paying for legal services and notes his office never requests payments over the phone. He plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate the source of these scams.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A fake online article falsely depicted Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler, where she allegedly stormed out over questions about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. This fabricated story exemplifies a growing scam trend that uses artificial intelligence to create deepfake content featuring well-known Australians to promote fraudulent investments. ASIC reports that such schemes are becoming increasingly sophisticated and prevalent online.

According to ASIC's latest research, scammers are constructing elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, positive reviews, websites, and advertisements to lure investors. Last year, the regulator took down 19,400 scams, representing a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and finance presenter Alan Kohler are among the most commonly impersonated Australians. ASIC advises consumers to verify financial services licenses and check ASIC's public registers before investing, while Kohler argues that platforms distributing such content should face heavy fines.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
A proposed class-action lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco accuses Oura, the popular smart ring company valued at $11 billion, of false advertising regarding its sleep-tracking capabilities. The suit alleges that Oura's rings, which cost $300 and up, cannot accurately measure sleep stages as claimed and instead rely on unreliable artificial intelligence that performs no better than random guessing. The company markets its devices as capable of detecting what only hospital sleep labs can see, including REM and deep sleep stages, and claims 95 percent accuracy compared to clinical labs, but the lawsuit contends the rings lack the necessary sensors and electrodes to measure brain activity properly.

Oura disputes the allegations, stating it stands behind its scientific research and accuracy claims. The company says its rings estimate sleep stages using multiple physiological signals including heart rate, movement, and temperature, and that its sleep-staging technology has been validated in peer-reviewed studies. However, experts note that consumer sleep wearables provide estimates rather than medical-grade measurements and should not be overemphasized. This lawsuit follows a previous class-action claim against Oura alleging the company collected sensitive personal information without customer consent.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments. The group operates a data leak site and has victimized organizations across multiple countries. Researchers identified exposed infrastructure revealing that Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks against ten target organizations between mid-April and late May 2026. The ESXi ransomware variant encrypts virtual machine files using ChaCha20 encryption while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can access ransom demands.

In the first attack cluster, Aurora operators deployed custom tools like esxi_finder.py to scan for VMware infrastructure and used Cursor Agent to perform standard exploitation tasks including VPN setup, network scanning, domain enumeration, and NTLM relay attacks. The operators imposed strict restrictions on the AI agent, forbidding DCSync attacks, account lockouts, and adding new computer objects to domains. A second cluster of Aurora activity was identified with medium confidence, using different methods including SQL Server exploitation and S3 bucket exfiltration across eight victim organizations in six countries.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A major Pizza Hut franchisee filed a lawsuit in Texas alleging that the chain's mandatory adoption of Dragontail, an AI-powered delivery management system, caused severe operational problems and over $100 million in damages. Chaac Pizza Northeast, which operates approximately 111 Pizza Hut locations across the Northeast, claims that after the 2024 rollout, delivery performance plummeted when DoorDash drivers gained real-time visibility into kitchen operations. Drivers began batching orders and waiting up to fifteen minutes for multiple deliveries to accumulate, causing pizzas to arrive cold and late. The franchisee also alleges drivers could see tip amounts and payment methods, influencing which orders they accepted. Before the system was implemented, Chaac maintained over 90 percent on-time delivery rates and double-digit sales growth.

The lawsuit contends Pizza Hut failed to provide adequate training, refused to address the problems, and breached the franchise agreement by mandating continued use of the flawed software. In New York City specifically, Chaac's year-over-year sales plummeted from positive 10.19 percent to negative 9.78 percent following the rollout. The company is seeking over $100 million in damages plus attorneys' fees. Pizza Hut stated it is reviewing the claims and will respond through appropriate legal channels but declined further comment.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Scammers have been sending personalized emails impersonating Terry Gross and other "Fresh Air" staff members to solicit money from potential interview guests. The fraudulent messages, which appear highly professional and reference targets' specific work, claim to offer interview opportunities but later request payment for production costs, typically around $250. Several authors, entertainers and public figures have reported receiving these emails, including historian Jennifer Black from Misericordia University and comedian Bruce Vilanch. WHYY, NPR and "Fresh Air" have confirmed they are investigating the scam and clarified that they never charge guests to appear on their programs.

According to cybersecurity experts, artificial intelligence has made these impersonation scams more sophisticated and convincing than traditional fraud attempts. Red flags include requests for payment, the use of personal Gmail accounts instead of official addresses, and claims that major hosts are personally handling logistics. Experts recommend verifying suspicious interview requests through official organization channels rather than responding directly to suspicious emails and note that potential victims should be wary of any payment requests.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Israel established and funded a fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute for Public Policy to influence artificial intelligence chatbots through propaganda. Between August 6 and 14, the site published 124 reports totaling over 560,000 words, formatted as neutral research to present Israel's positions on topics including Palestinian torture, war crimes, and starvation in Gaza. The reports were designed to optimize how AI systems would cite and reference the content. A media production company filed the site with the US Justice Department as material distributed for the Israeli government under foreign agent registration requirements.

The operation was part of a broader campaign funded by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government and routed through European advertising firm Havas Media. Israeli officials have reportedly expressed doubt about the campaign's effectiveness, with one saying the government paid substantial money but the situation worsened. Recent polling shows American support for Israel has declined significantly, with Palestinians now viewed more favorably and increasing percentages believing Israel's actions constitute genocide. Researchers warn the project demonstrates how foreign governments and others can manipulate training data for AI systems in ways that are difficult to fact-check.

incidents.summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, and others have filed separate lawsuits against AI music generators Udio and Suno. The companies are accused of copying thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models. The record labels claim both companies have been deliberately secretive about their training data and that their business model relies on exploiting copyrighted material on a massive scale. The lawsuits name specific artists whose work was allegedly used, including The Beatles, Michael Jackson, and many others.

To support their claims, the record labels demonstrated they could repeatedly recreate versions of famous copyrighted songs by using specific prompts in both AI generators. For example, prompting Suno with details about Mariah Carey and holiday music produced a near-identical copy of "All I Want for Christmas Is You," while an Udio prompt about 2004 alternative rock generated a song that replicated Green Day's "American Idiot" lyrics and melody. The lawsuits were filed in New York and Massachusetts and include a thumb drive of AI-generated music examples as evidence.

incidents.summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, which had been accused of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence model. The dispute centered on allegations that Udio created music similar to existing hits, such as The Temptations' "My Girl," without permission or compensation. Under the new licensing agreements, Udio will launch a platform next year trained exclusively on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize, stream, and share songs they create. Financial terms of the settlement were not disclosed.

This settlement marks Udio's first licensing agreement with a major record label and reflects the growing tensions between entertainment companies and AI startups over copyright protection. Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, lets users generate original songs from text prompts. The company said artists can opt into the new platform and will receive compensation, though specific details remain undisclosed. UMG also announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
# Summary

State Farm's legal team apologized for filing court motions containing fabricated legal cases, citations, and quotes in a lawsuit brought by Los Angeles homeowner Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga. The plaintiff sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire left her home uninhabitable, and subsequent water damage and approval delays prevented repairs from being completed. She and her husband exhausted their savings, declared bankruptcy, and lost their home to foreclosure. State Farm lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted using an AI tool called Irys that incorrectly generated seven nonexistent case citations across eight filings, along with false case titles and quotes.

Lead counsel Kenneth Katel apologized to the court and plaintiff, accepting responsibility for the filings and stating his firm updated its AI policies. The case is scheduled for trial in October. This incident reflects a broader trend, with 41 percent of law firms now using generative AI. A Paris-based database has identified nearly 1,900 legal hallucination cases worldwide, mostly in the United States, prompting increased scrutiny of AI use in the legal profession.

stories.Headline: Electoral court sets new standards for AI deepfakes
stories.Summary:
Brazil's highest electoral court established new guidelines for identifying artificial intelligence-generated deepfakes in political content ahead of October elections. The ruling came from a case involving opposition candidate Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who displayed AI-created images of his imprisoned father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, at his party's convention in July. The deepfake showed the former president endorsing his son's campaign against current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to lead a coup.

The court voted 4-3 to not punish Senator Bolsonaro, determining the deepfake was shown at a private party event rather than a public political advertisement. However, the court voted 5-2 to formally define what constitutes a deepfake in political advertising as synthetic content created or altered using artificial intelligence technology that realistically reproduces a person's image, voice, or speech. These standards will apply to thousands of campaign ads broadcasters must air before the October 4 election, during 14 minutes of daily airtime designated for political commercials.

stories.Headline: Nvidia buying artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face for $13 billion
stories.Summary:
Chipmaker Nvidia is acquiring Hugging Face, an artificial intelligence software platform, for approximately $13 billion. Hugging Face is used by over 18 million developers, researchers, and creators who share more than 3 million models, 500,000 datasets, and 1 million applications on the platform. More than 200,000 companies also use the service. Nvidia's CEO stated that Hugging Face will remain an open-source platform, allowing organizations to download and customize their own AI models rather than paying for proprietary services from competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic.

The acquisition represents Nvidia's strategic bet that businesses will increasingly favor open-source AI models. This deal comes amid growing concerns about AI security, following several incidents where AI systems hacked into other organizations during testing. The $12.93 billion purchase includes $1 billion for employee retention. Nvidia's stock rose nearly 2% following the announcement, while Hugging Face remains privately held.

stories.Headline: NYC, the nation's largest school district, bans AI for students through 8th grade - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
stories.Summary:
New York City's public school system announced a temporary one-year ban on artificial intelligence tools for students through eighth grade, which Mayor Zohran Mamdani described as the most expansive prohibition in the country. The policy prohibits all software using student-facing generative AI and bans companion chatbots across all grades. Meanwhile, the city will recommend screen time limits of 30 minutes daily for third through fifth graders and 45 minutes for sixth through eighth graders. Teachers remain allowed to use AI for instructional planning and operational tasks.

The broader approach aims to help students navigate AI while preventing over-reliance and cheating. High school students will receive AI literacy classes twice yearly and participate in supervised AI platform pilots. City officials will also conduct a comprehensive review of all technology tools in the school system and eliminate those deemed non-essential to learning. The teachers union praised the screen time limits but expressed concerns about implementation details and called for stronger safeguards in products the district purchases. Students are scheduled to return to classrooms the following week.

stories.Headline: Lawmakers propose oversight for state, local agencies using AI - Yahoo
stories.Summary:
Nevada lawmakers are proposing legislation to establish basic standards for how state and local government agencies use artificial intelligence. Democratic state Senator Dina Neal recommended the committee pursue this action due to concerns about the lack of oversight and potential risks associated with integrating AI systems without legal requirements. The proposed legislation would require transparency around AI use and prevent bias in automated decision-making. Several Nevada agencies, including the Department of Employment, Training, and Rehabilitation and the Department of Motor Vehicles, have already implemented AI systems. Some people have reportedly been denied benefits and unable to speak with a human during appeals processes.

The nine bill draft requests, including the AI oversight proposal, were approved at an August 27 interim Government Affairs Committee meeting. The legislation will be considered during the 2027 Legislative Session beginning February 1. State Senator Edgar Flores emphasized the importance of ensuring humans ultimately make important decisions rather than relying solely on automated systems. Senator Neal said the state needs to audit agencies and determine how many errors have occurred where human response was needed but did not happen. Lawmakers anticipate facing resistance from state and local agencies when the bill is discussed.

stories.Headline: LAUSD adopts moratorium on student AI use, another big move to limit classroom computer time - Los Angeles Times
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Unified School District has implemented a moratorium on student use of generative artificial intelligence on school devices for the current school year. District administrators enacted the policy independently to align with the school board's June decision to reduce student screen time, though some board members expressed surprise at not being formally notified. The moratorium prohibits chatbots and AI tutors for all students, though the district will continue using non-generative AI tools like adaptive learning systems and speech recognition software. Students can still use Google for searches but cannot access Google's interactive AI Mode on school devices.

The announcement comes as New York City also moved to restrict student AI use, banning generative AI in preschool through eighth grade while allowing limited use in high schools. Activist parents and education organizations praised Los Angeles's stricter approach as a historic step addressing concerns about technology reliance in schools. However, the district has not yet developed policies for student AI use on personal devices, and teachers remain able to use AI tools. Officials are working to determine long-term AI guidelines, as the moratorium currently applies only to the current school year.
